los.text: Describe the main causes, pathophysiology, clinical findings and investigations in abnormal pubertal development or a child presenting with failure to thrive (FTT)
sessions: Clin 3: Abnormal patterns of growth and puberty
los.html:
Faltering growth (failure to thrive)

Definition (NICE NG75)
  • Weight falling across ≥1 centile space (birth weight <9th centile), ≥2 spaces (9th–91st), ≥3 spaces (>91st), or weight below 2nd centile
  • or newborn losing ≥10% birth weight.
Causes
  • Inadequate intake (commonest): feeding difficulties, poor technique, insufficient breastmilk, oromotor problems (CP, cleft), neglect/poverty, maternal depression.
  • Inadequate absorption: coeliac, CF, cow's milk protein allergy, IBD, short bowel.
  • Increased requirements: congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, chronic infection (HIV, TB, UTI), hyperthyroidism, malignancy.
  • Abnormal utilisation: inborn errors of metabolism, chromosomal (Turner, Down), endocrine (GH deficiency, hypothyroidism: these affect height more than weight).
Assessment
  • Plot on UK-WHO growth charts (weight, length/height, head circumference; correct for prematurity until 2 years)
  • Mid-parental height
  • Feeding/dietary history
  • Observe a feed
  • Stools
  • Vomiting
  • Developmental and social history
  • Examination (dysmorphism, signs of systemic disease, neglect).
Ix(targeted; most need none)
  • Urine dipstick/culture (UTI)
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • LFT
  • TFTs
  • Coeliac serology (tTG IgA + total IgA)
  • CRP/ESR
  • Ferritin
  • Sweat test
  • Karyotype in girls with short stature (Turner).

Abnormal puberty

Precocious
  • Girls <8, boys <9.
  • Girls usually idiopathic central
  • Boys more often pathological (CNS tumour, CAH, testicular tumour).
  • Central (gonadotropin-dependent: ↑ LH/FSH) vs peripheral (gonadotropin-independent).
Delayed
  • No signs by 13 (girls) or 14 (boys).
  • Constitutional delay (commonest; FHx, delayed bone age), chronic disease (IBD, coeliac, anorexia, CF), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann: anosmia), hypergonadotropic (Turner, Klinefelter).
IxLH/FSH, oestradiol/testosterone, TFTs, prolactin, bone age (X-ray left hand), karyotype, MRI brain, GnRH stimulation test.

los.text: Describe the implications of neglect and deprivation in the aetiology of growth and developmental abnormalities in childhood
sessions: Clin 2: Neglect and deprivation: Effects on childhood growth and development
los.html:
Neglect
  • Persistent failure to meet a child's basic physical and/or psychological needs (food, warmth, shelter, hygiene, supervision, medical care, emotional responsiveness) likely to impair health or development.
  • The most common reason for a child protection plan in the UK.
DeprivationPoverty, poor housing, food insecurity; emotional deprivation (institutional care, parental mental illness, substance misuse, domestic abuse).
Effects on growth
  • Undernutrition → faltering weight then height.
  • Psychosocial short stature ("deprivation dwarfism"): emotional deprivation → functional ↓ GH secretion; growth recovers rapidly when removed from the environment (catch-up growth confirms diagnosis).
  • Untreated medical conditions (missed appointments, poor dental health, untreated infections).
Effects on development
  • Language delay (lack of stimulation), cognitive and educational underachievement, poor social skills, attachment disorders (insecure/disorganised), behavioural problems, emotional dysregulation.
  • Early life adversity affects brain development (adverse childhood experiences (ACEs): ↑ later physical and mental illness).
Recognition
  • Dirty/unkempt
  • Inappropriate clothing
  • Recurrent infestations
  • Severe nappy rash
  • Missed immunisations/appointments
  • Faltering growth with weight gain in hospital
  • Developmental delay
  • Attention-seeking or withdrawn behaviour.
ResponseDocument growth, holistic assessment, early help/family support, safeguarding referral if significant harm; Health visitors and Flying Start (Wales).

los.text: Describe the gastrointestinal causes, pathophysiology and investigations of faltering growth in childhood
sessions: Clin 4: Chronic GI disorders in childhood
los.html:
CauseFeaturesIx
Coeliac diseaseAfter gluten introduction; diarrhoea/steatorrhoea, abdominal distension, irritability, wasted buttocks, iron deficiency, short staturetTG-IgA + total IgA (on gluten); duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) if needed
Cystic fibrosisMeconium ileus, steatorrhoea (pancreatic insufficiency), recurrent chest infections, salty sweatNewborn heel-prick (IRT), sweat test (Cl⁻ >60), genetics, faecal elastase
Cow's milk protein allergyInfants; vomiting, diarrhoea ± blood, eczema, colicClinical; elimination diet trial
Gastro-oesophageal reflux diseaseVomiting, feed refusal, irritability, archingClinical; pH study if severe
Pyloric stenosis2–8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry, olive mass; hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosisUSS; pyloromyotomy
IBD (Crohn's)Older children; growth failure may precede GI symptoms; abdominal pain, diarrhoea, perianal disease, ↑CRPFaecal calprotectin, endoscopy
Short bowel syndrome, chronic liver disease, giardiasis, lactose intolerance, Hirschsprung's
Pathophysiology
  • ↓ intake (pain, vomiting, anorexia)
  • ↓ absorption (mucosal damage, pancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency)
  • ↑ losses (protein-losing enteropathy)
  • ↑ energy needs (inflammation; cytokines also suppress IGF-1).
Baseline IxFBC, ferritin, U&E, LFTs/albumin, CRP/ESR, coeliac serology, stool microscopy/culture, faecal calprotectin/elastase.

los.text: Describe how theoretical approaches to truth-telling relate to specific clinical scenarios
sessions: MHS 1: Knowledge of risks/truth-telling in relation to (legal) consent
MHS 2 Truth telling and trust in medicine (ethics)
los.html:
Truth-tellingDuty to give patients honest information about their condition, prognosis and treatment, including errors.
Theoretical approaches
  • Deontology (Kant): lying is always wrong; violates autonomy and treats people as means. Strict duty of honesty.
  • Consequentialism: tell the truth if it produces the best outcomes; may justify withholding if truth causes serious harm (criticised: hard to predict, undermines trust).
  • Virtue ethics: honesty as a core virtue, exercised with compassion and practical wisdom (how and when to tell).
  • Principlism: autonomy (patients need truth to make decisions) vs beneficence/non-maleficence (avoid distress). Historically therapeutic privilege (withholding to prevent serious harm) – now very narrowly applied in UK law (Montgomery).
  • Care ethics/relational: honesty within relationships, considering family and cultural context.
Clinical scenarios
  • Breaking bad news: use SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy/summary); check how much the patient wants to know (right not to know).
  • Family asks you not to tell (collusion): explore their concerns, but the patient has the right to information; ask the patient what they want.
  • Medical errors: statutory/professional Duty of Candour (GMC/NMC; Wales: Health and Social Care (Quality and Engagement) (Wales) Act 2020): be open, apologise, explain, put right.
  • Placebos, uncertainty about prognosis, children (age-appropriate honesty), cultural preferences for family-centred disclosure.
Consent linkValid consent requires material risks to be disclosed (Montgomery 2015); truthfulness underpins trust in the profession.
